slides.title: You walk into the kitchen. And you forget why.

slides.body:
You get up with a clear plan. You walk into the next room.

And the plan is gone. You stand there, trying to remember what you came for.

Psychologist Gabriel Radvansky had students carry objects through a virtual building, then quizzed them on what they were holding.

Those who had just walked through a doorway forgot more than those who walked the same distance inside one room.

slides.kicker: Then he tried it in real rooms.
slides.body:
Same result. Walking through a door made memory worse.

Going back to the first room didn't help either. It wasn't the place that mattered. It was the crossing.

slides.kicker: A door is an event boundary.
slides.body: Your mind splits life into episodes. A doorway tells it one has ended, so it files the old one away.

In 2021, researchers in Australia and the UK tested it again in virtual reality. With nothing else to think about, doorways made no difference.

The effect only appeared when people were also doing a hard counting task in their heads.

slides.kicker: The door isn't the real problem.
slides.body:
A busy mind is. When your attention is already full, any small change of scene is enough to push a thought out.

The researchers' advice: if you want to beat the doorway, keep a focused mind.

slides.lead: We often blame the moment we lost something.
slides.accent: But it was usually already slipping, because our mind was too full to hold it.

slides.line: Save this for your next trip to the kitchen.

caption:
You walk into the kitchen and forget why you came. Psychologists call it the doorway effect, and they've tested it in real and virtual rooms.

The twist: doors mostly trip us up when our minds are already full. 🚪

What's the last thing you forgot the moment you walked into a room?
